name: Wild food & mushrooms
desc: Rules for picking wild food, nettles, dandelions, berries, wild garlic, chestnuts, and mushroom safety

s: Only eat what you're 100% sure about. If you have any doubt, leave it.
Learn plants in person, with someone who knows them or on a guided walk. Pictures alone aren't enough.
Try one new plant at a time, and only a little the first time.
Don't pick next to busy roads, on sprayed fields, or where dogs are walked.
Take only a little from each spot and never pull up whole plants.
Check the rules: in nature reserves picking is often not allowed, also in the Netherlands.
d: Don't trust folk tests (‘animals eat it, so it's safe’)

s: Wear gloves. Pick only the top 4–6 young leaves, in spring and early summer, before the plant flowers.
Rinse them in a colander (still with gloves).
Cooking, blanching or drying takes the sting away completely.
Use them like spinach: in soup, with eggs, in pasta or stews.
Dried leaves make a tea.
Easy to recognise: one yellow flower per hollow stem, milky sap, and a rosette of toothed leaves.
Young leaves: in salads (a bit bitter) or cooked like spinach.
Flowers: fritters in batter, or sprinkled over a salad.
Roots: wash, slice, roast until dark and use as a coffee substitute.
Pick away from roads and lawns that may have been sprayed.

guides.w: Which ones, and which to avoid
s: Blackberries: on thorny brambles, from August. Ripe when black and soft.
Raspberries and wild strawberries: easy to recognise, early summer.
Elderberries: dark purple clusters in late summer. Only eat them cooked (jam, syrup): raw ones can make you sick.
Rose hips: the red fruit of wild roses after flowering. Remove the hairy seeds inside; good for syrup and tea.
Any berry you don't know for sure: leave it.
d: Never eat white berries or unknown berries
Yew (red berries on a dark, needled hedge): the seeds and leaves are deadly

guides.t: Wild garlic and its deadly look-alikes
s: Wild garlic grows in carpets in damp woods in spring, with white star-shaped flowers.
Each leaf grows on its own thin stalk straight from the ground.
Crush a leaf: it smells strongly of garlic. But the smell stays on your hands, so check each leaf separately.

Look-alikes: lily of the valley (2–3 leaves wrapped around one stem, bell flowers) is poisonous; autumn crocus (leaves in a bunch, no garlic smell) is deadly; the young leaves of arum are poisonous too.
Pick leaf by leaf, never by the handful.
d: No garlic smell from that exact leaf: don't eat it

s: Sweet chestnut: a husk covered in many fine, sharp spines, like a hedgehog. Inside 2–3 flat-sided nuts with a little tassel on top.
Horse chestnut (conker): a thick husk with a few short, thick spikes and one round, shiny nut. It's poisonous.
Cut a cross in the shell of sweet chestnuts and roast them in embers or a pan for 15–20 minutes, or boil them.
Acorns are edible only after soaking in many changes of water for days to remove the bitter tannins.
Every year people die from mushrooms they were sure about. Only eat a wild mushroom after an expert has checked it, in person.
In Italy, the local ASL health office checks mushrooms for free (ispettorato micologico). Elsewhere, ask a local mushroom society.
Pick the whole mushroom, including the base under the soil: that's where deadly ones show their cup.
Keep each kind separate, in a basket, not a plastic bag.
Never eat wild mushrooms raw, and eat only a small portion the first time.
Picking mushrooms is not allowed in many nature areas, also in the Netherlands.
d: No identifying by app, photo or picture, including the drawings in this guide
Folk tests don't work: silver spoons, peeling, or animals eating them prove nothing
guides.src: Poison-centre advice (NVIC / Centro Antiveleni) and Italian ASL mushroom inspectorates

guides.w: Learn these so you never touch them
s: Death cap: greenish to yellowish cap, white gills, a skirt-like ring on the stem and a sack-like cup at the base. Often under oaks. Most mushroom deaths are caused by this one.
Destroying angel: all white, with the same ring and cup. Easily mistaken for a field mushroom.
Deadly webcap: orange-brown, in pine woods. Kidney damage starts days later.
Funeral bell: small, brown, in groups on rotting wood. Same poison as the death cap.
Small white mushrooms in grass (fool's funnel): poisonous and look like edible ones.
Symptoms of the worst ones start 6–24 hours later, after which people feel better before getting worse. By then the liver is already damaged.
d: Never eat a white mushroom with a ring and a cup at the base

guides.w: Someone ate a wild mushroom and feels ill
s: Call 112, or a doctor straight away, even if they feel better after a while.
Also call if someone ate a mushroom nobody had checked, even if they feel fine.
Keep any leftovers, peelings, and the rest of the mushrooms, or take photos: they help identify the poison.
Find out who else ate it: they need checking too.
Tell them when it was eaten and when the symptoms started. Late symptoms (after 6 hours) are the most dangerous.
d: Don't wait to see if it passes
